Singular inputs and zero covectors in hyperfunction kernels

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI; no independent review. CC0.

A kernel can carry a singularity at its output even when the input contributes no nonzero covector. When two kernels meet, their common covector can also be zero. We retain these cases while constructing kernel action and contraction for hyperfunctions. Proper addition then gives convolution, including unbounded supports and a direct proof of associativity.

Write . All spaces below are Euclidean open sets, all maps used for substitution are real analytic, and scalar integration uses Lebesgue density. The actual operations and proofs are supplied by Analytic substitution for hyperfunctions, Theorems 4, 7 and 10 and Proposition 5; Tensor directions and admissible hyperfunction products, Theorems 1, 4, 6 and 7; and Integrating hyperfunctions over proper fibers, Theorems 2 and 6 and Propositions 7–8.

A relation with its support zero section

For a kernel , use the primed relation Its joint covector is nonzero, but either endpoint separately may vanish. Put The covectors displayed in and are nonzero. These projected sets need not be closed without further support information.

Lemma 1 (the closed extended relation). The set is closed in the full product cotangent space.

Proof. For a convergent sequence whose limiting joint covector is nonzero, a subsequence of nonzero joint covectors lies in the closed set ; a sequence of joint zeros cannot have this limit. If the limiting joint covector is zero, every base point in the sequence belongs to , because a hyperfunction vanishing near a point has empty wavefront there. The support is closed, so the limit belongs to the added zero section. The priming sign is a linear homeomorphism and preserves this argument.

For closedness, take output pairs in the right side converging to a nonzero pair. Their base points lie in a compact subset of . Properness of places the chosen fiber points in a compact subset of . If infinitely many pairs use the first line, pass to that subsequence and use closedness of and of the supports. Otherwise write their matched input covectors as . Finite unions of proper support sets are proper. The wavefront of a sum is contained in the union of the wavefronts, so the same exclusion applies to admissible sums. Linearity of product and integration proves the assertion. The actual distributional comparisons for projection pullback, product and proper integration identify (A2) with the previously constructed distributional action in Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Theorem 5.

A compactly supported input always satisfies the support part of (A1). Alternatively, properness of over allows arbitrary input support. The stated intersected-support hypothesis also covers cases in which neither stronger condition holds. For analytic , only the first line of (A3) remains.

Proper convolution and its surviving directions

Theorem 5 (proper convolution). Let , and suppose addition is proper on . Define Then The support sum is closed and the wavefront bound is locally closed off zero. Formula (Q1) is also the action of the kernel on . It agrees with distributional convolution and, for compact analytic functionals, with

Proof. The map is an analytic linear diffeomorphism with absolute determinant one. Its inverse is . Properness of addition on the support is therefore exactly the required properness for the projection in (Q1). The actual coordinate and integration operations define it.

Under , a tensor covector becomes Integration requires , and the output covector is nonzero. Each factor must therefore contribute a nonzero wavefront covector; neither support-zero term survives. This proves (Q2). Properness bounds the two base points over compact output sets, while the two covectors are the same bounded output covector. Closedness follows by taking subsequences, with nonzero limit. The same argument without covectors proves that the support sum is closed.

Tensor naturality and product pullback identify The exact submersion formula gives . Thus is empty. Theorem 2 applies, and (Q5) proves equality with kernel action, including its normalization.

For compact , the inverse-Jacobian formula, with determinant one, and the compact projection pairing give (Q3) on every admissible holomorphic germ. This is the convolution of Proposition 7 in Analytic tests and real carriers. The exact comparisons of tensor, analytic coordinate change and proper integration give distributional agreement for general proper supports as well.

One compact factor suffices for properness: if remains in a compact set and, for example, remains in a fixed compact set, then is bounded; closedness completes the argument. The theorem also covers two unbounded supports, such as the two nonnegative half-lines.

Theorem 6 (the convolution algebra on proper supports). Every admissible pair satisfies where . If total addition is proper on three nonempty supports, both iterated convolutions are defined and More generally, for finitely many nonempty supports with proper total addition, every parenthesization is defined and has the same value. Any zero input gives zero in each expression whose intermediate convolutions are defined.

Proof: compact inputs and localization. For compact analytic functionals, the two iterated germ pairings defining the tensor agree and are associative. Pairing with proves commutativity. Differentiation in either variable gives the same derivative of this test, with the same minus sign. Pairing a point delta in the first variable gives , which is precisely translation. Repeated pairing with proves all compact-input parenthesizations. These statements use the complete tensor and transport proofs of Proposition 7 in the analytic-functional lesson.

Apply Lemma 4 to an admissible pair and a relatively compact output patch . On the inverse image of under addition, the tensors and agree. To verify this at a point, either one coordinate lies outside its enlarged support, where both versions of that factor vanish locally, or both coordinates lie in the enlarged supports. In the latter case Lemma 4 puts both coordinates in , where the factors agree. Locality of tensor and coordinate pullback, followed by restriction compatibility of proper integration, gives The enlarged-support condition ensures every convolution used in this comparison is defined. It proves commutativity and derivative identities locally from their compact versions. Derivatives preserve support and local agreement, so the same replacements work for every fixed . Gluing proves them globally. For the translation formula, the same reasoning can keep the already compact factor : choose the second representative to agree near . Its pairing gives the stated translation locally and hence globally.

Proof: three factors. If all supports are nonempty, fixing one point in the third support proves properness for addition on the first two supports; a compact pair-sum set translates to a compact total-sum set. Similarly the other pair is proper. Addition on is proper: lift any sequence with total sum in a compact set to . Total properness gives a convergent subsequence of the lifts. The intermediate support sum is closed by pair properness. This proves compactness of the inverse image, including its closedness. The actual support of is a closed subset of that sum, so its further convolution is admitted.

Choose the three compact replacements from Lemma 4, with enlarged supports . The same properness argument applies to these enlarged supports. Put This is open. The tensors and agree over the inverse image of under pair addition: for a contributing pair, choose making its total sum lie in . Lemma 4 then puts its two coordinates in . The other points have a factor zero locally, as in (Q8). Hence the two pair convolutions agree on .

The support of their difference misses , so its sum with misses . Also, a contributing sum from and can be lifted to coordinates in ; Lemma 4 puts the third coordinate in . There vanishes. The support bound thus gives, on , Every sum and difference used here is admissible because its support is contained in a finite union of the proper enlarged support sums. Repeating the argument for the other grouping gives on . Compact associativity and gluing prove (Q7).

For a finite number of factors, fixing points in the omitted nonempty supports proves properness of every subsum. Its support sum is closed. At any split into two blocks, lift a bounded total sum to the original tuple to prove properness of addition of the two block support sums. Thus every parenthesization is defined. Two adjacent regroupings are equal by the three-factor argument applied to the three block convolutions whenever their supports are nonempty; their total support addition is proper by the same lifting argument. If a block convolution is zero, the corresponding regrouping equals zero by bilinearity, with admissibility already ensured by the containing support sums. Repeatedly moving parentheses to the left, by induction on the number of leaves, connects every parenthesization to the fully left-associated one. This proves the finite assertion.

The nonempty-support qualification is useful: a zero third factor does not imply properness for an unrelated first pair. When the needed pair convolutions exist, bilinearity gives the expected zero without that false implication.

For a zero-dimensional factor, the space is a point or empty. Hyperfunctions on a point are scalars, with no nonzero covectors. Tensoring, integration and convolution reduce to scalar multiplication; empty factors give zero. The displayed constructions and bounds have these interpretations.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (basic) — an output-axis singularity. Let be a compactly supported hyperfunction on , let on , and let be any compactly supported hyperfunction on . Find .

Solution. The input-normal set is empty, since exact projection covariance gives covectors with . Tensor and product naturality identify . The first line of (A3) is therefore essential.

Exercise 2 (intermediate) — translating a singular input. For , calculate its action on any hyperfunction and its primed relation.

Solution. Theorem 5 identifies its action with . The support graph has one fiber point for each output, so the properness condition holds for every . Exact submersion covariance gives The relation and both endpoint-normal exclusions agree with this translation formula. Applying the inverse translation and its wavefront bound also proves equality of the translated wavefront sets.

Exercise 3 (basic) — testing the normal exclusion. On , take and input . Does Theorem 2 apply?

Solution. Exact projection covariance gives all covectors , , over . After priming, contains both nonzero directions at zero, as does . Condition (A1) fails. In fact the proposed product would contain the same-variable delta square. The theorem supplies no such product; proper fiber support alone does not supply the missing normal exclusion.

Exercise 4 (advanced) — all outer directions with middle covector zero. In one-dimensional factor spaces set Compute the contraction and explain every part of (C4).

Solution. The set is empty, because its joint covectors are , . Thus (C2) holds, even though is nonempty. The joint support has , so it is proper. Formula (C6), tensor naturality and integration of the middle delta give A point delta in two dimensions has every nonzero ordinary covector: its localized Fourier transform is a nonzero constant. Hence its analytic wavefront also contains every nonzero covector, and cannot contain more. In the matched relation for (E3), the middle covector is always zero, because the first component of every covector of is zero. If both outer components are nonzero, both factors have nonzero joint covectors. If one outer component is zero, the appropriate factor contributes its support zero, producing a term in (C8). Together these give the whole punctured outer cotangent plane. Removing the middle zero would lose all of it.

Exercise 5 (advanced) — convolving infinite point measurements. Suppose point-carried functionals have the convergent expansions Find the moments of , prove convergence, and give a nondistribution example in one dimension.

Solution. The exact tensor germ pairing gives coefficients The point-moment theorem in the analytic-functional lesson gives, for every , bounds and . The coordinatewise binomial identity therefore gives Taking half of any prescribed radius proves the required every-radius bound. Absolute convergence on a sufficiently small complex neighborhood, followed by the Cauchy derivative bounds for the test, justifies regrouping the double series. Equivalently the complete tensor germ theorem gives the same pairing and coefficients.

In one dimension choose . The bounds above hold since . Formula (E6) gives The last identity compares the coefficient of in . Every is positive. A point-supported distribution has finite order on a compact neighborhood. Theorem 1.1 of the supplied jet lesson makes it vanish on tests whose derivatives through order vanish at that point. Subtracting a cutoff times the degree- Taylor polynomial therefore expresses its pairing as a finite derivative sum. Uniqueness of the analytic moment expansion makes every higher coefficient zero. Thus the convolution just constructed is not a distribution.

Exercise 6 (intermediate) — properness is a separate condition. Compare the formal convolutions of the two functions and with the convolution of two copies of , where is the indicator of the positive half-line.

Solution. For opposite half-lines, the fiber over zero contains , , and is unbounded. Addition is not proper. The ordinary positive integrand for their convolution has infinite integral on each output fiber, so this example does not define a convolution by (Q1). For two nonnegative half-lines, and in a compact set bound both variables. Addition is proper, and Indeed the allowed first variable is for , and there is no allowed interval for . Endpoint choices affect neither distribution. The output is analytic off zero and fails to be smooth at zero. Ordinary wavefront projection and real Fourier conjugation symmetry force both ordinary directions there, and hence both analytic directions. The bound (Q2) attains precisely these directions.
